label: A Map of the Whole Theory
notes: These closing pages step back from proofs and ask what the book has built. Optimal transport began as a logistics question and matured into a language for couplings, distances between measures, curvature, dynamics, and inequalities. The lecture treats the conclusion as a map, marking both settled territory and the open frontiers that remain ahead.

label: Five Pillars Built Through the Book
notes: We name the five load-bearing ideas: couplings and the Kantorovich relaxation, the Wasserstein metric on probability measures, the synthetic reading of Ricci curvature, gradient flows in that metric, and the functional inequalities that follow. Each pillar was developed separately, yet the chapter insists they are facets of one structure.

label: Pillar One: Couplings and Kantorovich
notes: Everything starts with the relaxation from maps to plans. Allowing mass to split makes the problem a linear program with a clean dual, restoring existence where Monge's formulation failed. Kantorovich duality turns transport cost into a supremum over potential functions, the device reused throughout the book to prove sharp statements.

label: Pillar Two: Wasserstein Geometry
notes: The optimal cost with quadratic price defines a genuine distance on probability measures with finite second moment. Benamou and Brenier recast it as a least-action problem, so the metric space carries geodesics, a formal Riemannian structure, and a notion of velocity field. This is the stage on which the remaining pillars are built.

label: Pillar Three: Synthetic Ricci Curvature
notes: Lott, Sturm and Villani encode a lower Ricci bound as convexity of entropy along Wasserstein geodesics. The curvature-dimension condition needs no smooth manifold, only a metric measure space, so curvature survives limits and singular spaces. This is the book's deepest structural payoff and the seed of much current research.

label: Pillar Four: Gradient Flows
notes: Many diffusion equations are steepest descent of an energy in Wasserstein geometry. The heat equation descends entropy; porous-medium and Fokker-Planck flows descend their own functionals. The minimizing-movement scheme makes this rigorous, giving existence, contraction estimates, and a variational reading of irreversible dynamics in one framework.

label: Pillar Five: Functional Inequalities
notes: Displacement convexity converts geometric curvature bounds into analytic inequalities. Log-Sobolev, Talagrand transport-entropy, Brunn-Minkowski and isoperimetric statements all emerge from one convexity principle along geodesics. The chapter highlights this unification: a single geometric input produces a whole family of sharp analytic outputs that once seemed unrelated.

label: How the Pillars Interlock
notes: The synthesis is that no pillar stands alone. Couplings build the metric, the metric hosts geodesics, convexity of entropy along those geodesics is curvature, curvature drives the gradient flows, and the flows certify the inequalities. The concept map makes this circular dependence visible as a single connected diagram.

label: Open Frontier: Sharp Regularity and MTW
notes: Smoothness of the optimal map depends delicately on the cost. Ma, Trudinger and Wang isolated a fourth-order curvature tensor of the cost whose sign governs regularity. On manifolds it ties transport smoothness to the geometry of cut loci, leaving sharp thresholds and general cost regularity wide open.

label: Open Frontier: RCD and Hilbertian Refinement
notes: The curvature-dimension condition allows Finsler behaviour, which the heat flow should not see. Adding infinitesimal Hilbertianity, that the heat flow is linear, singles out the Riemannian-like RCD spaces. Stability, structure theory, and the boundary between branching and non-branching geometry remain very active open questions today.

label: Open Frontier: Numerics and Applications
notes: The analytic theory leaves computation underdeveloped. Entropic regularization and Sinkhorn iteration made large transport problems tractable and connect to machine learning, imaging, and economics. Sharp rates, debiasing, scaling to high dimension, and faithful discretization of curvature and gradient flows form a fast-moving applied frontier.

label: Closing: An Unfinished Atlas
notes: The conclusion frames optimal transport as a maturing but unfinished atlas. Old questions of logistics now power a synthetic geometry of measures, yet regularity, nonsmooth structure, and computation keep the subject open. The invitation is to read each theorem as both a settled result and a doorway to the next problem.
